title: Architecture
summary: Four groups. The application is what people use; the other three exist to test it, measure it and report on it.

layers.name: What you see: browser controls
layers.summary: Address bar, tabs and buttons. Our code.

layers.name: What you see: websites in tabs
layers.summary: The open web. Sandboxed, with no access to Ferrum's own functions.

layers.name: Ferrum engine
layers.summary: The new Rust code: manages tab views, applies the safety rules, puts idle tabs to sleep and measures.

layers.name: Shared base
layers.summary: Settings, ids and record formats used by every engine part.

layers.name: Microsoft WebView2
layers.summary: The Chromium engine (same as Edge) that draws each website.

layers.name: Windows 11
layers.summary: The operating system: process readings and links to other apps.

groups.name: Application
groups.purpose: What people use: the Ferrum app itself. The measurement parts sit here because they run inside the app; the benchmark uses their output.
groups.flow: you click → browser controls → engine checks the rules → WebView2 loads the site → it shows in the tab

groups.name: Benchmark
groups.purpose: Runs the same workloads on Ferrum, Chrome, Edge and a plain Tauri app, many times, in random order.
groups.flow: harness → launch browser → run workload → record numbers

groups.name: Testing & quality
groups.purpose: Proves each feature works and stays working: unit, end-to-end and security tests, plus automatic checks on every change. No component of its own.
groups.flow: change → tests + check scripts → green → commit

groups.name: Research & analysis
groups.purpose: Turns raw numbers into statistics, charts and the paper. No claims without data.

footnote.text: Planning tooling, not part of Ferrum: this plan portal, which Claude keeps in step with the wiki.

browser_design.title: How the browser will look
browser_design.summary: You chose option A: tabs across the top, the website in the middle, and a Ferrum panel on the right that shows memory, CPU, sleeping tabs, blocked sites and the network log. No AI assistant; light and dark mode.
browser_design.sample_note: Numbers, sites and log lines are examples. Nothing is measured yet.

callouts.label: Tabs on top
callouts.text: Rounded tabs across the top of the window, with the Windows 11 minimise, maximise and close buttons at the right.

callouts.label: Address bar with a lock
callouts.text: Back, forward and reload, then a rounded address bar; a lock shows the site uses a secure connection.

callouts.label: Shield with blocked count
callouts.text: A shield button next to the address bar; its badge counts what the blocklist stopped on this page.

callouts.label: Ferrum panel
callouts.text: A panel on the right (about 352 pixels wide) with memory and CPU of all tabs, sleeping tabs and blocked sites; a button hides it.

callouts.label: Sleeping tabs
callouts.text: A tab Ferrum put to sleep to save memory shows a moon and greyed text; the panel says when an idle tab will sleep.

callouts.label: Network log: addresses only
callouts.text: The panel lists this tab's requests (method, address, status, size), never page content, with a button to open the log folder.

components.title: Browser controls
components.summary: The window you use, built in P2 and P3: tabs, address bar, bookmarks, sidebar, settings, downloads, backup and the Graphite look ([the look you chose](ref:adr-0033)). P4 added block and crash messages, a "not secure" bar, site settings, SmartScreen and program warnings, and permission questions. P5 adds switches for measuring and the network log.

connects.what: sends tab commands: open, close, go to, back, reload
passes your settings changes to the safety rules
loads and saves settings
hands outside links to Windows after you confirm

components.title: Websites in tabs
components.summary: Any website you open, each in its own view. Untrusted: treated as the attacker and sandboxed. Its view is created by Ferrum, so it should have no bridge to the app at all (checked in P2); if one appeared, every command would be refused.

connects.what: should have no bridge to the app (checked in P2); any command would be refused
asks to open pages, pop-ups, downloads and permissions

components.title: Tab & view manager
components.summary: Creates, shows, hides and closes each website view. Trusted; the only part that talks to WebView2 directly, with low-level code Rust cannot fully check. Since P4 it also stops frames, notices crashes, gives a site its own engine, keeps SmartScreen on and holds permission requests until you answer. In P5 it reads page timings and network calls.

connects.what: asks whether each navigation, download or permission is allowed
creates, moves, shows, hides and pauses tab views
reports page timings and which processes are Ferrum's
passes network call details (no content)
reports each tab's address, title, loading and errors

components.title: Security policy
components.summary: Decides what is allowed: sites, pop-ups, downloads, permissions, links to other apps. Trusted; refuses when unsure. Since P4 it decides every page load, redirect, frame and pop-up, and when to ask you before a site uses your camera, microphone, location, notifications or clipboard. A benchmark-only build can skip site rules; the app never has it.

connects.what: reads the rule settings
reports how long each decision takes

components.title: Tab sleeping
components.summary: Watches idle tabs and memory, then hides, pauses or unloads idle tabs and restores them when needed. Trusted. Four policies to compare: none, fixed idle time, memory pressure, adaptive. Never unloads the tab you are using. Risk: unloading could lose what you typed. Before P7, background tabs are only hidden.

connects.what: tells it to hide, pause, unload or restore a tab
records every sleep and wake decision
reads tab-sleeping settings

components.title: Measurement: memory, CPU and timings
components.summary: Inside the app: records memory and CPU of Ferrum's processes, startup and page timings, and tab sleeps and wakes, as data files; off unless you switch it on. Built so far: the file format, counting only Ferrum's processes, the memory and CPU meter, startup and page-load timing, tab state changes, and writing it all during use. A cross-check only. Trusted.

connects.what: reads memory and CPU counters per process
sends memory readings and a low-memory signal
exports per-run data; lends its process-reading code
exports data files for analysis

components.title: Measurement: network log
components.summary: Writes every tab's network calls to a folder you can review: full address, method, status, kind and size, and whether Ferrum blocked it. Never headers, cookies or page content. Off unless you switch it on; files older than 14 days are deleted. Built in P5; it misses requests with no reply and a service worker's own requests. Trusted.

connects.what: gives request logs to check each trial loaded the same things
uses the shared record format

components.title: Core library
components.summary: The shared base every Rust part uses: settings with defaults and checks (since P4 also your blocked and allowed sites lists and three ways to keep sites apart; since P5 the measuring and network log switches), record formats, the local database for history and bookmarks, and the passphrase-locked backup file ([decision](ref:adr-0032)). Trusted.

components.title: Microsoft WebView2
components.summary: Microsoft's Chromium engine (the same one inside Edge), already installed on Windows. It draws every website and the browser controls. Not ours. Ferrum relies on its sandbox; P4 tests saw no page process shared between two sites; that it protects as well as Chrome's is not checked yet (P6).

connects.what: reports navigations, pop-ups, downloads, permissions and crashes
loads and draws the websites

components.title: Windows 11
components.summary: The operating system. Not ours. Gives memory and CPU readings per process, groups a test's processes for counting, and opens outside links in other apps. Which Windows low-memory signal to use is decided in P7.

components.title: Benchmark harness
components.summary: Starts each browser fresh, runs the same scripted workloads many times in random order, and measures from outside so every browser is measured the same way. Trusted; not shipped. Risk: proving Ferrum's helper processes are counted fairly; not checked yet (checked in P6).

connects.what: starts Ferrum fresh and isolated for each trial
starts the plain Tauri app the same way
starts Chrome and Edge and drives the workloads
reads memory, CPU and process groups
hands over raw results, archived unedited

components.title: Plain Tauri app (comparison point)
components.summary: The simplest Tauri app that shows one web page, with no Ferrum features. Trusted; not shipped. Comparing with it separates Ferrum's own cost or savings from the cost of Tauri and WebView2.

connects.what: shows one page with plain Tauri, no Ferrum parts

components.title: Chrome and Edge
components.summary: The browsers Ferrum is compared with. Not ours. Run with their normal resource-saving features on, never switched off to favour Ferrum; their settings are recorded in every trial.

components.title: Statistics and figures
components.summary: Python scripts that turn archived raw results into statistics, charts and reports for the paper. Trusted; not shipped. They read only archived runs, so every figure traces back to its data.

components.title: Plan portal (this site)
components.summary: The site you are reading. A planning tool, not part of Ferrum: a read-only portal with seven tabs that shows Claude's plain-language text and each check script. You start it with one PowerShell script and approve things in Claude Code.
